finds.title: Public Law 107-296, Homeland Security Act of 2002
finds.author: United States Congress
finds.evidence_quote: There is established a Department of Homeland Security, as an executive department of the United States within the meaning of title 5, United States Code.
finds.line: Congress created the Department of Homeland Security as an executive department, giving it the mission that now covers the border and immigration workforce.
finds.about: This is the public law that set up the Department of Homeland Security. It was approved on November 25, 2002. Title I sets up the department and states its primary mission, which begins with preventing terrorist attacks within the United States.
finds.because: The new department brought the border and immigration agencies together under one workforce, the same workforce whose names were later published.

finds.title: Warner, Kaine Push ICE to Require Agents Identify Themselves, Limit Use of Masks and Face Coverings During Enforcement Operations
finds.author: Sen. Mark R. Warner and Sen. Tim Kaine
finds.source: Office of Sen. Mark R. Warner (warner.senate.gov)
finds.evidence_quote: Across the country and in Virginia, masked ICE officers and agents without clearly visible identification as law enforcement have been arresting individuals on the streets and in sensitive locations, such as courthouses.
finds.line: Senators Warner and Kaine wrote to ICE and DHS asking for their rules on face coverings and on revealing officer identities during immigration arrests.
finds.about: Two senators released this letter and press statement in May 2025. They said masked ICE officers without clear identification were making arrests on streets and at courthouses. They asked DHS and ICE for policies, guidance and training materials on masks and officer identity.
finds.ties_to: officials who mask up and wear plain clothes in American cities
finds.because: The letter put the masking question on the record in Congress, setting up the fight over whether agents' identities should be hidden or public.

finds.title: Cybersecurity Incidents
finds.author: U.S. Office of Personnel Management
finds.evidence_quote: In 2015, OPM announced two separate but related cybersecurity incidents that have impacted the data of Federal government employees, contractors, and others
finds.line: In 2015, OPM announced two separate but related cybersecurity incidents that affected the data of federal government employees, contractors, and others.
finds.about: OPM, the federal personnel agency, announced the incidents in 2015. There were two of them, and they were separate but related. They affected the data of federal employees, contractors, and other people.
finds.ties_to: records of more than 41,000 DHS employees taken by hackers
finds.relation: earlier instance of the same action
finds.because: The 2015 breach showed that stolen federal workforce data could reach millions of people, which framed later worries about who holds staff records and how well they are guarded.

finds.title: Congress Passes the Daniel Anderl Judicial Security and Privacy Act
finds.author: Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts
finds.evidence_quote: It also will allow federal judges to redact personal information displayed on federal government internet sites and prevent publication of personal information by other businesses and individuals where there is no legitimate news media or other public interest.
finds.line: Congress passed the Daniel Anderl Act, letting federal judges redact personal details on government websites and limiting publication of that information by others.
finds.about: Congress passed the act on December 16, 2022. It lets federal judges redact personal information shown on federal government internet sites. It also bars businesses and individuals from publishing that information where no legitimate news media or other public interest exists.
finds.ties_to: laws protecting law enforcement personal information
finds.because: This law gave Congress a working model for limiting publication of officials' personal details, and later bills on officers' names borrowed the same idea.
